title: Mikasa: lunch aboard the flagship and the problem of supply
dek: During the blockade of Port Arthur, 156 people aboard Mikasa suffered food poisoning. The shortage of food supply ships was recognised as a problem of that war, yet the fleet’s first dedicated food supply ship did not enter service until 1924.

sections.title: The flagship off Port Arthur
paragraphs: During the Russo-Japanese War, the battleship Mikasa took part in blockade operations off Port Arthur. She was an armoured Japanese warship and the flagship of the Combined Fleet—the ship carrying its commander. The Russian squadron was in its base; the Japanese ships operated outside it. They too needed an anchorage where they could undergo maintenance and replenish supplies. From 10 May 1904, Mikasa was undergoing maintenance at a forward base among the islands south of China’s Liaodong Peninsula.
The ship was still there on 30 May. Japanese historian Akinori Ishihara described that day’s lunch and the food poisoning that followed in his study of naval supply.

Rice and barley, soup with dried radish and tea were on the breakfast menu. More rice for lunch, with stewed canned salmon and seaweed, pickles and barley tea. For dinner, hardtack and roast beef with potatoes. At an anchorage where fresh food was scarce, Ishihara considers this a fairly ordinary menu.

sections.title: After lunch
paragraphs: The canned salmon had spoiled: its storage life had been exceeded. After lunch, 156 people aboard Mikasa fell ill. This happened on the flagship, at its own forward base, and the cause was food from the ship’s menu.

Food poisoning also occurred aboard other Japanese ships in May and June. Among the reported causes were canned goods, fried tofu (soybean curd) and mouldy bread; sometimes the offending food could not be identified. Aboard Mikasa, efforts were made to serve food that had been cooked: stewed, fried or boiled. The crew had to eat every day, despite all the difficulties of delivery and storage.

sections.title: From transport ship to the crew’s meal
paragraphs: At the start of the war, two auxiliary vessels, Matsuyama Maru and Fukuoka Maru, were prepared to supply food. Deliveries to the forward forces were planned roughly every six days. But the warships often operated in dispersed groups, and two supply vessels proved too few. From August 1904, Kotohira Maru and other ships were brought into this work.

The additional ships helped with transport, but they lacked enough equipment to preserve the food. They could not carry sufficient provisions. Even the few days’ voyage from the Japanese naval base at Sasebo to a forward base made it difficult to keep bread, vegetables, meat and fish fresh. Refrigeration technology already existed, but its installation aboard ships was only beginning.

The shortage of food supply vessels was recognised as one of the weaknesses of supply during the Russo-Japanese War. The auxiliary transports of 1904, however, were not yet the dedicated fleet food supply ships that appeared later. The first such ship in the Japanese navy, Mamiya, entered service in 1924. The second, Irako, followed on 5 December 1941. Ishihara argues that, against the backdrop of the Japanese fleet’s victory at Tsushima in 1905, the supply shortcomings exposed by the war were not adequately reflected in subsequent naval policy.

Feeding the crew during battle called for a different arrangement. On 27 May 1905, the first day of the Battle of Tsushima, hardtack and a drink made from kudzu starch were kept ready on Mikasa’s upper, middle and lower decks. Sailors could eat and drink as needed. Rice balls were handed out for dinner at five in the afternoon.
Regular meal arrangements resumed at eight that evening, when fighting paused for the night. The seriously wounded received special food: eggs, condensed milk and porridge.

limitations: The lunch and number of people taken ill are described in Ishihara’s 2024 study. The original medical volume has not been checked separately; 156 counts people taken ill, not deaths. No causal link has been established between the spoilage of this batch of canned salmon and the shortage of ships.

The dates for Mamiya and Irako refer to dedicated fleet food supply ships. Auxiliary vessels were already supplying food in 1904. The assessment of how the navy absorbed the war’s lessons is Ishihara’s.

title: Banks and Cash Houses in Dairen: How Credit Worked
dek: In Dairen, a cash house could arrange a loan for a familiar business client over the telephone. Yet to borrow from a bank itself, it pledged property. What made a telephone loan possible?
perspective: From bank clerk Sun Yaoting’s memoir and Guo Xipu and Sun’s account of Dalian’s cash houses

sections.title: You had to know who was calling
paragraphs: In the late 1920s and early 1930s, a Chinese business owner with a good reputation could arrange a loan by telephone in Dairen, as Dalian was known under Japanese rule. The lender was a qianzhuang: a private cash house that accepted deposits, made loans and transferred money to other cities. Making the call was easy. Becoming someone who would get the money afterwards was another matter.

Guo Xipu and bank clerk Sun Yaoting described this practice. Sun had worked in finance since 1930, including at the joint Japanese-Chinese Longkou Bank. In their recollection, small and medium-sized Chinese businesses often preferred a cash house to a foreign bank, where loans were harder to obtain and procedures more complicated. They were willing to pay more for a loan they could actually get.

The telephone did not make credit equally available to everyone. A cash house considered the borrower’s reputation and adjusted its terms to the availability of money in the market. Sun separately recalled how difficult it was for an ordinary resident to obtain a loan without adequate security. In the same city, one borrower could get money after a call while another found the door all but closed.

sections.title: Behind the call was a property mortgage
paragraphs: There was another side to this convenience: the cash house itself depended on a bank. Merchants left money with it for only short periods, and deposits from residents were few. If depositors withdrew their money before loans were repaid, the house’s own funds might fall short. Sun and Guo were explicit: without bank support, a cash house risked being unable to meet its payments.

A qianzhuang would therefore generally mortgage property to a bank and arrange an overdraft: the right to draw more from an account than it held. For its own client, it might make borrowing as simple as a telephone call. To borrow itself, it provided something quite tangible as security. Personal trust and a bank’s demand for collateral fitted comfortably into the same chain.

Nor was the borrower the only person whose reputation mattered. Depositors looked at the wealth and standing of a cash house’s owner and shareholders. Trust in these people brought money into the till, from which loans could then be made. Connections based on a shared home province helped too: Shandong cash houses chiefly served businesspeople from Shandong. But Sun qualified this picture. Shared economic interests also held people together, and the groups’ membership changed.

sections.title: A document worth more than property
paragraphs: There was another kind of security that, according to Sun and Guo, a bank would accept more readily than property: a railway consignment note for grain. Some well-funded cash houses were set up specifically to trade soybeans, gaoliang and other grain. After buying the goods, they handed the transport document to a bank and obtained cash against it. The grain was still on its journey, but the document already made borrowing possible.

Here the credit relationships acquire names. Sun listed the firm Xingji, managed by Xin Bofen, and Yifahe, managed by Wang Xinzhai, among the major clients of banks and cash houses. These were well-funded participants in grain trading and oil milling. When necessary, they themselves helped their creditors meet day-to-day payments. Who came to whose aid depended on who had money available at the time.

Yet a consignment note said nothing about where the borrowed money would go. Sun and Guo recalled that cash houses acting as grain-trading agents also used such credit to speculate on the currency exchange. Some grew rich quickly; others were ruined. Their account does not identify particular transactions by Xingji or Yifahe, and we cannot assign this course to either firm. The lending mechanism itself is clear, however: reliable security helped a borrower obtain money, but the borrower could still put it to risky use.

sections.title: Who now decided whether to lend?
paragraphs: This network depended on being able to trade, transfer money and reach an agreement with a creditor. After full-scale war between Japan and China began in 1937, the Japanese authorities tightened their control over trade. According to Sun and Guo, restrictions on the grain market undermined the trading agents’ business; Chinese cash houses’ overseas transfers ceased, and some establishments closed or changed their line of business.

Their account of wartime regulations includes a particularly telling detail. A commercial loan of 50,000 yuan or more required prior permission from the Japanese administration. The threshold was 100,000 for an industrial loan and 30,000 for an overdraft. Agreement between lender and borrower, even with adequate security, was no longer enough: a transaction of this size needed official approval. By 1944, according to the same account, only eight Chinese cash houses remained in Dalian.

More people stood behind a telephone loan than could be heard on the call. Behind the lender were depositors and a bank; behind money borrowed against a consignment note was the grain trade. War changed the conditions for the entire chain. You could keep your good name, have goods to offer and find someone willing to lend, then still have to wait for permission. The question was no longer just whether someone trusted you with the money, but whether the loan would be allowed.

limitations: This article draws on retrospective accounts by participants in financial life, recorded and edited by Huang Benren: Sun Yaoting’s memoir and the joint account by Guo Xipu and Sun. Sun contributes to both texts; they are not two wholly independent testimonies.

Credit mechanisms, wartime restrictions and the number of cash houses are described only as given in these accounts. Individual contracts, the named firms’ accounts and original Japanese regulations have not been checked. Naming a firm as a major borrower does not establish that it engaged in every type of transaction described here.
